A **WARNING** is raised when the projected 15-minute demand reaches **1,125 kW**, which is **90% of the 1,250 kW contract capacity**.

**Why that level:**
- The contract capacity is 1,250 kW [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Contract capacity].
- The warning line is set at 90% of that contract, i.e. 1,125 kW [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-04_glossary.md#EM-04 Glossary > Billing and demand terms > Warning line].
- The purpose is to give an early lead-up signal before demand actually hits the contract. A projected demand at or above 1,125 kW raises WARNING, and per SOP-01 the next group of loads is held until it clears, so the plant can avoid breaching the 1,250 kW limit (which would trigger a penalty at 2× the contract price) [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-01_monday_startup.md#SOP-01 Monday Start-up > Procedure > Group 1: utilities].

So 1,125 kW is deliberately chosen as a 10% safety buffer below the contract, giving operators time to shed loads before an actual exceedance.

- **Up to 10% over the contract** (i.e., up to 1,375 kW): the excess is billed at **2× the period's contract price** [unverified citation removed]
- **Beyond 10% over the contract** (above 1,375 kW): the excess is billed at **3× the period's contract price** [unverified citation removed]

I found the exact explanation. Here's the answer.

The load forecaster predicts the **change from an anchor** rather than the absolute demand level because of a fundamental limitation of tree models (the primary model is LightGBM).

**The core reason: tree models cannot predict a value above anything they saw in training.** In the plant's training data, demand rarely exceeded the 1,250 kW contract, so a model trained to predict the *level* would never learn to forecast values above that ceiling — it simply caps out. The first version of the forecaster used a level target and **missed the exceedances entirely** [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model].

By predicting a **delta** instead, the model can *add* a heat-driven or start-up-driven increment on top of the current load, so it can still warn about an exceedance even when that exceedance is above anything in the training set [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model].

**How the anchor is chosen:**
- Short horizons (15 min to 3 h): the anchor is the last completed 15-minute interval [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]
- Day-ahead: the anchor is the same time last week [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model]

All five models (profile, linear, hgb, lightgbm, ensemble) deliberately share this same delta-from-anchor framing, so any performance differences come from the model itself, not from the target definition [source: docs/forecasting.md#Load forecasting > Model comparison].

In short: predicting the change lets the forecast ride on top of the current load and still break above the contract limit, which a level-based model structurally cannot do.

On a hot afternoon when the forecast warns demand may exceed the **1,250 kW contract**, operators should follow **SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling**, backed by **SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response** if a warning actually fires.

**1. Act on the forecast probability, not just the projection.** The forecast gives P(exceed) for the next hour: 20% or more raises a WARNING, 50% or more raises an ALARM. These warnings give time to act *before* the 15-minute interval average is affected — most useful on hot afternoons when chillers and the cooling tower rise together. [source: docs/knowledge/energy-management/EM-02_demand_management.md#EM-02 Demand Management > Forecast-based warnings]

**2. Pre-cool before the peak (move cooling energy earlier).** Run the chilled water system ahead of the peak window so the building/lines are already cool, avoiding adding new load during the peak. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Purpose]

**3. Defer or pause non-essential / deferrable load.**
- Pause the **EV Charging Bank** before hot-afternoon peaks; resume only once projected demand falls back below 1,125 kW. [source: docs/knowledge/equipment/EQ-13_ev_charging.md#EQ-13 EV Charging Bank Manual > Energy-saving notes]
- Avoid starting new loads (e.g. new injection-mold cycles, reflow runs) in the peak window.

**4. During the peak, monitor every interval and shed in playbook order if WARNING/ALARM fires.**
- Monitor projected demand every interval. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak]
- If a warning/alarm is raised, follow **SOP-03** and shed load in the playbook order. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-03_demand_exceedance_response.md#SOP-03 Demand Exceedance Response]
- If the pre-cooling margin allows, raise the chilled-water setpoint by **+1 °C** (about 4% of present chiller load) to trim chiller demand without sacrificing cooling. [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Procedure > Step 6: during the peak]

**5. Never shed these critical loads**, even under ALARM:
- The server room
- Injection molders running mid-cycle
- Reflow ovens with boards inside

[source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-06_heat_wave_precooling.md#SOP-06 Heat Wave Pre-cooling > Never shed]

**In short:** pre-cool ahead of the peak, defer deferrable load (notably the EV bank), watch the forecast's P(exceed), and if a WARNING/ALARM fires, shed in the SOP-03 playbook order while nudging the chiller setpoint up — but never shed servers, mid-cycle molders, or ovens with boards.

## The 16 June 2025 Start-Up Incident

**Peak demand:** The plant hit a peak of **1,324.4 kW** in the 15-minute interval starting **08:15** on 2025-06-16 — about **6% above** the 1,250 kW contract capacity. [data: get_demand]

**What caused it:** At roughly 07:57, **10 machines started simultaneously within a 3-minute window** (07:57–08:27), totalling **805 kW of rated capacity**. The affected equipment was:
- **3 Reflow Ovens** (RF-01, RF-02, RF-03)
- **4 Injection Molders** (IM-01, IM-02, IM-03, IM-04)
- **Chiller 2** (CH-02)
- **Air Compressor 2** (AC-02)
- **Wave Soldering Machine** (WS-01)

This is the documented "Monday morning simultaneous start" scenario S2. [data: list_detections]

**What a 15-minute stagger would have achieved:** Re-simulating the same morning with the machines started 15 minutes apart would have:
- Cut the peak from **1,324.4 kW down to 1,141.5 kW** (a reduction of **182.9 kW**)
- Brought demand **below the 1,250 kW contract**, eliminating the exceedance
- Avoided a penalty of up to **NT$6,652 (US$208)** [data: whatif_staggered_start]

In short: the spike was a classic cold-start coincidence of heavy loads (reflow ovens, molders, a large chiller and an air compressor) all energizing at once. Spacing the start-ups by 15 minutes would have flattened the peak enough to stay under contract and avoid the demand exceedance penalty.

## Detection

- **Detection date:** 3 September 2025 (night-load baseline detector, flagged on 9 September) [data: list_detections]
- **Size:** ~18.1 kW above the usual night base load, running around the clock across AC-01, AC-02 and AC-03 [data: list_detections]
- **Estimated annual impact:** about NT$652,462 (US$20,389)/year [data: list_detections]

## Inspection Procedure (SOP-04 Compressed Air Leak)

**Step 1 — Confirm the signal**
- Check the night load of AC-01, AC-02 and AC-03 over the last nights.
- Confirm the meters are reporting (SOP-07); a stale meter or kWh register reset can imitate a change.
- Check that no production activity at night explains the increase (e.g. a molder running).

**Step 2 — Choose the time for the walk-down**
- Do the ultrasonic walk-down in a quiet period, ideally at night or on a Sunday, when machine noise is low and the leak is the largest part of the flow.

**Step 3 — Ultrasonic walk-down**
- Use an ultrasonic leak detector along the main headers and branches.
- Start with the areas with the most pneumatic use, in particular injection molding.
- Check fittings, quick couplers, hoses, filter and regulator units, drain valves and blow-off nozzles.
- Check the air dryer area and the compressor room.

**Step 4 — Tag**
- Tag each leak with a numbered tag at the location.
- Record location, type, and estimated size (small, medium, large).
- Photograph the tag where practical.

**Step 5 — Repair**
- Isolate the section where possible and depressurize it.
- Replace the faulty fitting, hose or valve.
- Re-pressurize and recheck with the detector.
- Remove the tag and record the closure.

Per SOP-05 (Power Factor Check), the usual cause is a **capacitor bank that is out of service** — check for a tripped breaker or a blown fuse on the capacitor bank [source: docs/knowledge/sop/SOP-05_power_factor_check.md#SOP-05 Power Factor Check > Purpose].
